extraction.name: DAQUAR
extraction.description: DAQUAR is a VQA dataset consisting of 6795 training and 5673 testing QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset, featuring exclusively indoor scenes. It is one of the smallest VQA datasets and was the first major VQA dataset released.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Multiple VQA datasets were collected using different methods: NLP algorithms applied to image captions (COCO-QA), human annotators asking free-form and region-specific questions (Visual Genome), crowd-sourced human-generated QA pairs (FM-IQA, COCO-VQA), and synthetic shape-based question generation (SHAPES). DAQUAR was based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images from Microsoft COCO dataset (328,000 images), NYU-DepthV2 Dataset, YFCC100M (Flickr100M), and synthetic cartoon imagery. COCO contains 91 common object categories with over 2 million labeled instances and an average of 5 captions per image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected. For The VQA Dataset, annotators generated ten answers per question. For FM-IQA, human judges assessed answers using two metrics: determining whether the answer was produced by a human or not, and rating answers on a 3-point scale (totally wrong=0, partially correct=1, perfectly correct=2). For Visual Genome, two modes were used: free-form (annotators asked any question) and region-specific (workers prompted to ask questions about specific image regions).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is 83.3% using AccuracyVQA. Inter-human agreement is especially poor for 'Why' questions, with over 59% having less than three annotators giving exactly the same answer. More than 13% of yes/no answers have both 'yes' and 'no' repeated by more than three annotators. Human accuracy on DAQUAR full dataset is 50.2%.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5 human annotated ground truth answers per question; The VQA Dataset: 10 answers per question; Visual Genome: average of 17 QA pairs per image
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: COCO-QA uses an NLP algorithm to automatically derive QA pairs from COCO image captions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: VQA datasets have strong language biases where questions severely constrain expected answers, making language a stronger prior than image features. Datasets tend to have biased distributions of question types and answers (e.g., 'yes' is more common than 'no' in COCO-VQA). Models trained on biased datasets perform significantly worse on balanced test sets.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Current VQA datasets are insufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has 'solved' VQA. They are not large enough (performance curves have not reached asymptote), are heavily biased toward language over image content, use evaluation metrics that treat all questions equally regardless of difficulty, and may be gamed by exploiting answer biases rather than true image reasoning. Binary questions and multiple-choice formats have additional limitations.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: VQA has potential to aid blind and visually impaired individuals by enabling them to query images on the web and in the real world. It could also improve human-computer interaction and enable image retrieval without metadata. However, current systems' over-reliance on language bias limits their deployment for real-world applications.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: VQA datasets are used for training and evaluating VQA algorithms. Use cases include object recognition, object detection, attribute classification, scene classification, counting, spatial reasoning, and common sense reasoning about images. Applications include aiding visually impaired users, human-computer interaction, and image retrieval. The paper recommends mean per-question-type performance for more nuanced benchmarking.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: SYNTH-VQA uses synthetic images to reduce natural image biases; Yin and Yang dataset built on SYNTH-VQA to eliminate answer biases; Visual Genome used region-specific question prompting to combat bias in free-form questions; SHAPES dataset is completely balanced with every question asked about each image
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: COCO-QA QA pairs generated automatically from COCO captions using NLP algorithm; COCO-VQA questions collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk with workers asked to 'Stump a smart robot' and separate workers providing 10 answers per question; Visual Genome used both free-form and region-specific annotation methods; Visual7W multiple-choice answers collected by prompting annotators to answer without seeing the image; DAQUAR-consensus collected additional ground truth answers for alternative evaluation

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: Using synthetic images, these biases can be reduced. Yin and Yang [42] is a dataset built on top of SYNTH-VQA that tried to eliminate biases in the answers people have to questions... The creators of Visual Genome combated this by also prompting workers to ask questions about specific image regions... Unlike other datasets, this means it is completely balanced and free of bias.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: In COCO-QA, QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions... Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to 'Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers... Two distinct modes of data collection were used to make the dataset. In the free-form method, annotators were free to ask any question about an image... Plausible answers are collected by prompting annotators to answer the question without seeing the image.
